## Why This Matters

A rapid dengue test advertised as "95% accurate" comes back positive during a low-transmission
month. Should the clinic treat it as near-certainty? Run the numbers: if 2% of tested patients
actually have dengue, the test catches 95% of true cases and falsely flags 5% of healthy ones, then
out of 1,000 patients about $0.95 \times 20 = 19$ true positives stand next to $0.05 \times 980 = 49$
false ones. A positive result means dengue only $19 / (19 + 49) \approx 28\%$ of the time.

The missing ingredient in the naive "95%" reading is the **prior** — how common the class is before
any evidence arrives. Bayes' rule is the machine for combining priors with evidence, and the family
of classifiers in this lesson and the next points that machine at classification by modeling what
each class *looks like*.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
A generative classifier learns a **portrait of each class** — a typical mango of each cultivar, say.
To label a new fruit it asks: *which portrait does this most resemble, weighted by how common that
cultivar is to begin with?* Logistic regression (L04) never draws a portrait; it only learns where
to put the fence between the classes. Same goal, opposite strategy.
:::

## Bayes' Rule

For a class $C$ and observed features $x$, Bayes' rule reads:

$$P(C \mid x) = \frac{P(x \mid C)\, P(C)}{P(x)}$$

| Term | Name | The question it answers |
|------|------|------------------------|
| $P(C)$ | **prior** | how common is this class, before seeing any evidence? |
| $P(x \mid C)$ | **likelihood** | how typical is this evidence *for* this class? |
| $P(C \mid x)$ | **posterior** | given the evidence, how probable is the class now? |
| $P(x)$ | **evidence** | how common is this evidence overall? (a normalizer) |

In the dengue story the prior is the 2% prevalence, the likelihoods are the test's behavior on sick
and healthy patients, and the posterior — the only number the patient cares about — is the 28%.

## From Bayes' Rule to a Classifier

Classification with Bayes' rule is one decision: compute the posterior for every class and **pick the
largest** — the *maximum a posteriori* (MAP) rule. Because every class's posterior shares the same
denominator $P(x)$, comparing posteriors never requires it:

$$\text{predict } \underset{C}{\text{argmax}} \; P(x \mid C)\, P(C)$$

Prior times likelihood, per class, compare. (To report honest probabilities rather than just a
winner, normalize the products so they sum to 1 — the lab does both.) Everything that follows is a
choice of **how to model the likelihood** $P(x \mid C)$.

## Generative vs Discriminative

L05 named the split; here is the machine behind it. A **generative** classifier models each class —
its distribution $P(x \mid C)$ and prior $P(C)$ — and lets Bayes' rule produce the boundary as a
by-product. A **discriminative** classifier (logistic regression, the Perceptron) learns the boundary
$P(C \mid x)$ directly and never models the classes at all.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  subgraph G["Generative (GDA, Naive Bayes)"]
    direction LR
    D1["Training data"] --> M1["A model of each class:<br/>P(x given C) and P(C)"]
    M1 -->|"Bayes' rule"| B1["P(C given x)<br/>and the boundary"]
  end
  subgraph D["Discriminative (logistic, Perceptron)"]
    direction LR
    D2["Training data"] --> M2["The boundary directly:<br/>P(C given x)"]
  end
```

| | Generative (GDA) | Discriminative (logistic) |
|---|------------------|---------------------------|
| Models | $P(x \mid C)$ and $P(C)$ | $P(C \mid x)$ directly |
| Learns | what each class *looks like* | what *separates* the classes |
| Training | per-class means + covariances (a formula, no iteration) | iterative gradient descent |
| Bonus ability | can *describe* (even generate) a typical class member | none — boundary only |

A generative model spends effort describing each class and gets the boundary for free; a
discriminative model spends everything on the boundary itself.

## Gaussian Discriminant Analysis

GDA makes the natural choice for continuous features: **model each class as a multivariate Gaussian**.
For class $C$ that means a mean vector $\mu_C$ (the class's center) and a covariance matrix
$\Sigma_C$ — and the covariance is the new power here. A single feature's spread is one number; a
covariance matrix also captures how features **vary together**. In the lab's mangoes, longer fruit
run heavier *within* a cultivar, so length and weight are correlated; the covariance encodes that
tilt, and the fitted Gaussian is a tilted ellipse rather than an axis-aligned blob.

Training is just arithmetic: estimate each class's mean and covariance from its training points, and
each prior from its share of the data. To classify a new point, evaluate each class's Gaussian
density at that point (the likelihood), multiply by the prior, and take the argmax — the MAP rule,
exactly as above.

## LDA vs QDA: One Covariance or Many

The one modeling choice left is whether the classes **share** a covariance matrix:

- **Linear discriminant analysis (LDA)** — assume *all* classes share one common covariance
  $\Sigma$. When the likelihoods differ only in their means, the curved parts of the Bayes boundary
  cancel and what remains is a straight line (a hyperplane). `LinearDiscriminantAnalysis` in
  scikit-learn.
- **Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA)** — give *each* class its own covariance $\Sigma_C$. The
  curvature no longer cancels and the boundary becomes a **quadratic** curve — an ellipse, parabola,
  or hyperbola — that can wrap around a class. `QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis`.

So the same generative recipe yields a linear classifier or a curved one purely from how many
covariance matrices you let it estimate. The lab draws both: LDA's straight boundary on the mangoes,
and — when the two classes have genuinely different covariance shapes — QDA's curve succeeding where
LDA's line cannot.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why a shared covariance gives a straight line (Optional)" collapse="true"}

Taking the log of $P(x \mid C)\,P(C)$ for a Gaussian gives a term
$-\tfrac{1}{2}(x - \mu_C)^{\top} \Sigma_C^{-1} (x - \mu_C)$ plus constants. The boundary between two
classes is where their log-scores are equal. With **per-class** $\Sigma_C$ the quadratic term
$x^{\top}\Sigma_C^{-1}x$ differs between the classes and survives the subtraction — a quadratic
boundary (QDA). With a **shared** $\Sigma$ that quadratic term is identical for both classes and
**cancels**, leaving only terms linear in $x$ — a straight boundary (LDA). One shared matrix versus
one per class is the whole difference between a line and a curve. The algebra belongs to a
statistical-learning course; the cancellation is the idea.
:::

## The Duality: A Generative Route to a Line

Look at what LDA produces: a linear boundary — the same kind of object logistic regression (L04) and
the Perceptron (L05) draw. Three methods, one shape, reached three ways: the Perceptron by chasing
mistakes, logistic regression by maximizing likelihood of the labels, LDA by modeling each class as a
Gaussian and applying Bayes' rule. On well-behaved data they often land on nearly the **same** line —
the lab checks that LDA and logistic agree on every test fruit. Naive Bayes (L07) is the other
generative classifier: it keeps Bayes' rule but, instead of GDA's full covariance, assumes the
features are independent — a different bet about $P(x \mid C)$, for a different kind of data.

## When to Use / When NOT to Use

- **Use it when:** features are roughly continuous and bell-shaped per class; you want a fast,
  closed-form classifier (no iteration); you value the bonus that the model *describes* each class.
- **Prefer LDA over QDA when** data is limited — one shared covariance is far fewer numbers to
  estimate than one per class, so QDA's extra flexibility costs data. There is a flexibility ladder
  here: a linear model (logistic, LDA) is the steady choice, QDA the flexible one that needs more
  data per class — the bias-variance trade Unit III makes precise (L09).
- **Avoid it when:** the per-class distributions are far from Gaussian, or strongly multi-modal — the
  single-bell-per-class assumption misleads.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Reaching for QDA by default.** Per-class covariances mean many more parameters; on small classes
  those estimates are noisy and QDA can lose to the simpler LDA. Match the model's flexibility to the
  data you have.
- **Forcing Gaussian on the wrong features.** Counts, categories, and heavy-tailed variables are not
  bell curves; a generative model with the wrong likelihood is confidently wrong. (Naive Bayes, L07,
  offers count-friendly likelihoods.)
- **Confusing "discriminant analysis" with "discriminative."** Despite the name, LDA/QDA are
  **generative** — they model each class. The word "discriminant" is historical.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"GDA or logistic regression?"** — They cost minutes; professionals often try both. Reach for LDA
when classes look roughly Gaussian, data is limited, or you want the closed-form speed and the
class-description bonus; prefer logistic regression when you have data to spare and want a model that
optimizes the boundary directly without a Gaussian assumption. On clean, Gaussian-ish data with a
shared covariance the two give nearly the same linear boundary — which is the duality this lesson is
built around.

**"LDA or QDA?"** — Start with LDA. It assumes one shared covariance, so it estimates far fewer
numbers and is steadier when classes are small. Move to QDA only when you have evidence the classes
have genuinely different spreads or orientations *and* enough data per class to estimate each
covariance — the lab shows a case where that switch lifts accuracy from 0.68 to 0.88.

**"Why assume a Gaussian at all?"** — Because two numbers per feature (a mean and a spread), plus the
correlations, summarize a class cheaply and train instantly, and for many continuous measurements the
bell curve is a decent approximation. When it is a bad one, you switch likelihoods (Naive Bayes for
counts/text, L07) or switch to a discriminative model that never makes the assumption.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Bayes' rule | posterior $\propto$ prior $\times$ likelihood |
| MAP rule | predict the class with the largest prior $\times$ likelihood |
| Generative | model each class $P(x \mid C)$ and $P(C)$, then apply Bayes' rule |
| GDA | model each class as a multivariate Gaussian (mean + covariance) |
| Covariance | captures how features vary together — the tilt a single spread misses |
| LDA | one **shared** covariance $\Rightarrow$ a **linear** boundary |
| QDA | a **per-class** covariance $\Rightarrow$ a **quadratic** boundary |
| Duality | LDA's line is the generative route to what logistic/Perceptron draw |
